source.title: Quantifying the Capability Boundary of DeepSeek Models: An Application-Driven Performance Analysis
source.authors: Kai-Kai Zhao; Zhao-Xiang Liu; Xuejiao Lei; Jiao-Jiao Zhao; Zhenhong Long; Zi-Peng Wang; Ning Wang; Mei-Juan An; Qing-Liang Meng; Peijun Yang; Min-Jie Hua; Chaoyang Ma; Wen Liu; Kai Wang; Shi-Guo Lian

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Numerical values from the figures are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across model sizes and reports whether larger models perform better in certain comparisons, but it evaluates task scores rather than held-out pretraining loss or scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates 22 models on A-Eval-2.0 and explicitly reports a general same-architecture, same-training-data size comparison, plus two smaller-versus-larger model comparisons and a QwQ-32B versus DeepSeek-R1 comparison. These bear on V6. The reported loss-scaling laws, fitted-curve extrapolations, compute-optimal allocations, architecture-shape effects, other modalities, and fit dependence are not tested. Other reasoning-enhancement, quantization, task-category, and subtask results are not rows unless they bear on downstream predictability by scale. Model-level plotted scores cannot be extracted from the supplied text.
record.test_reason: Not a scaling study. It evaluates off-the-shelf instruct, distilled, reasoning and quantized models on an application benchmark (A-Eval-2.0). It makes one qualitative claim relevant to V6: within identical architecture and training data, larger models score higher. That is a new setting (post-trained models, Chinese-heavy application tasks) with a coarse, curve-free result. No loss, fit or prediction is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct but mis-weighted. The paper's conclusion centres on reasoning-enhanced models not being universally superior, on capability-tier quantification and on a model-selection handbook. The scale finding ('larger parameter models demonstrate superior performance, aligning with the scaling law') is one minor observation in Section 3.1 and the abstract. The authors also say smaller models can match larger ones with better training and data, and they caveat biases from sample selection and scoring.
record.recipe_differences: Application-driven downstream benchmark evaluation and model comparisons, rather than held-out pretraining-loss measurements or scaling-law fitting.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors identify the Chinese-heavy evaluation data as a likely reason Qwen2.5-32B outperforms Llama-3.3-70B. They also caution that sample selection, data distribution, and evaluation criteria can bias results.

fits_no_version.finding: Across model families, parameter count does not order performance. Qwen2.5-32B beats Llama-3.3-70B before and after distillation, and QwQ-32B nearly matches DeepSeek-R1. The authors attribute this to training data and strategy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream rankings across model families with different data and training are not predicted by parameter count alone.

record.problems: The evidence is based on one application-driven benchmark and automatic scoring with expert review; the authors acknowledge possible biases from sample selection, data distribution, and scoring criteria. The supplied text does not provide exact score values for the scale comparisons, and plotted model-level values are unavailable.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1–6 contain model-level and task-level plotted scores, but the supplied text gives captions rather than extractable numerical values; these are not reconstructed. Other reported findings concern reasoning enhancements, quantization, or task-specific performance rather than the scale relationship in V6.

untested.parts: Predictability: no curve or fit of downstream score against parameters, compute or pretraining loss. No extrapolation. No per-size numeric scores in the text.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameters.
No other modality or regime fitted.

missing.what: Per-family tier grades by model scale across five task categories (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct C/C/C/D/C vs Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct A/B/A/B/B; Qwen2.5-14B vs 32B Instruct mostly equal tiers). This is the only per-size evidence in the text bearing on r1.

record.verdict_notes: Of the two scaling-law references the authors cite, [5] is Gao et al. on reward-model overoptimization, not a loss-scaling paper. Scores come from an LLM judge (DeepSeek-R1) with expert review. No uncertainty is reported. The evidence on V6 is weak and coarse.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute; power-law form and range.
Prediction of much larger runs from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
The study reports downstream benchmark-score comparisons, not performance as a function of pretraining loss, and does not fit or evaluate a predictive curve.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and curve bending.

rows.subject: Models with identical architectures and training data (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: Varied; exact sizes for this comparison not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared A-Eval-2.0 overall performance across parameter sizes
rows.value: Larger parameter models demonstrate superior performance
rows.note: Qualitative finding reported across the study's model comparisons; the text gives no exact scores or size-by-size values for this result.
rows.check: Qualitative statement only: no scores, no curve, no predictive fit. Supports monotone improvement within a family but cannot show 'predictably'. The authors give no listing of which pairs count as same-architecture, same-data. The Qwen2.5-Math 1.5B/7B models are differently trained from the Qwen2.5 14B/32B models.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Compared overall A-Eval-2.0 performance with the larger Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
rows.value: Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct outperforms the larger model; exact score not stated
rows.note: The authors suggest the Chinese-heavy evaluation data may explain this size-order exception.
rows.check: Cross-family comparison (Qwen2.5-32B vs Llama-3.3-70B) with different training data, which the authors blame for the result. It is not a scale comparison at fixed setup, so it does not bear on V6. Better recorded under fits_no_version.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, finding (5); Table 1 identifies the instruction-tuned models.

rows.subject: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B
rows.operation_detail: Compared overall A-Eval-2.0 performance with the larger DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B
rows.value: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B outperforms the larger model; exact score not stated
rows.note: The authors say this counterintuitive comparison likely reflects the predominance of Chinese data in the evaluation set.
rows.check: Same confound as r2: distilled Qwen-32B vs distilled Llama-70B differ in base model and pretraining data.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, finding (5); Table 1 identifies the distilled models.

rows.subject: QwQ-32B
rows.operation_detail: Compared overall A-Eval-2.0 performance with DeepSeek-R1
rows.note: The text reports the relative difference but does not provide the underlying scores here.
rows.check: QwQ-32B (dense) vs DeepSeek-R1 (MoE, 671B total, 37B active) differ in architecture, data and training. The authors cite it as evidence that training and data can offset size, not as a scale test. It is a selection-style comparison and not a V6 row.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, finding (6), reports 1.57%; Table 1 gives DeepSeek-R1 scale as 671B|37B.

relationships.condition: Within-family comparisons with same architecture and training data, application-benchmark scores of post-trained models
relationships.reason: The authors state that larger models score higher at identical architecture and data (r1). Table 2 tiers are broadly consistent, e.g. Llama 8B→70B rises from C/D to A/B. The evidence is coarse and qualitative, and predictability is untested.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models scored higher with architecture and data held constant, including Llama 8B to 70B improving from C/D to A/B tiers, without testing predictability.
